name.en: Drinking 5 litres of water every day

dose: 5 L plain water daily, spread through the day, on top of water from food (~0.5–1 L). Assumes a sedentary-to-moderately active adult in a normal indoor environment. An outdoor worker in a 42 °C Indian summer sweating 1–2 L/hour is a different case — for them 5 L may simply be replacement.

summary.en: Healthy kidneys can excrete roughly 0.8–1 L of dilute urine per hour, so 5 L spread across a day is usually handled without harm — you just urinate a lot. The problem is pace and context: gulping litres in a short window, or drinking far beyond sweat loss while eating little salt, dilutes blood sodium (hyponatraemia), which swells brain cells. For most desk-bound Indians 5 L is simply excess; for a construction worker in May it may be barely enough.
summary.hi: स्वस्थ किडनी हर घंटे करीब 0.8–1 लीटर पतला पेशाब बना सकती है, इसलिए दिन भर में फैलाकर 5 लीटर पानी पीने से आम तौर पर नुकसान नहीं होता — बस बार-बार पेशाब आता है। दिक्कत तब होती है जब थोड़े समय में ढेर सारा पानी गटक लिया जाए या पसीने से ज़्यादा पानी पिया जाए — खून में सोडियम पतला हो जाता है (हाइपोनेट्रीमिया) और दिमाग की कोशिकाओं में सूजन आ सकती है। ऑफिस में बैठने वाले के लिए 5 लीटर ज़्यादा है; मई की गर्मी में मज़दूरी करने वाले के लिए शायद बस पूरा।

indian_context: The '8 glasses' rule got inflated on Indian WhatsApp into '4–5 litres for glowing skin and detox'. Sweat loss in Indian summers (35–45 °C, high humidity in coastal cities) can genuinely reach 1–2 L/hour for outdoor workers, farmers and delivery riders — for them high intake with salt (nimbu-pani with namak, ORS, chaas) is protective. For an AC-office worker in Bengaluru, 5 L mostly means 10–12 toilet trips and washed-out sodium, especially if they are also on a low-salt diet or a thiazide BP tablet.
sources: ICMR-NIN Dietary Guidelines for Indians 2024 (water and fluid recommendations)
EFSA Panel on Dietetic Products. Scientific Opinion on Dietary Reference Values for water. EFSA Journal 2010
Hew-Butler T et al. Statement of the Third International Exercise-Associated Hyponatremia Consensus Development Conference. Clin J Sport Med 2015
Armstrong LE, Johnson EC. Water Intake, Water Balance, and the Elusive Daily Water Requirement. Nutrients 2018
caution: Do not do this if you have heart failure, chronic kidney disease, liver cirrhosis, SIADH, or take thiazide diuretics, SSRIs or carbamazepine — these impair water excretion and 5 L can cause dangerous hyponatraemia. Headache, nausea, confusion or a seizure after heavy water intake is an emergency. Never drink more than ~1 L in an hour unless you are replacing measured sweat loss.

timeline.headline: Kidneys flush the excess; 10–12 trips to the toilet

effects.note: Vasopressin (ADH) switches off and the collecting ducts stop reabsorbing water, producing very dilute urine (osmolality can fall below 100 mOsm/kg). This is the kidney working normally at its upper capacity, not damage.
The bladder fills every 60–90 minutes. Night-time trips (nocturia) begin if a large share is drunk after 7 pm, fragmenting sleep.
Plasma volume rises transiently after each large drink; blood sodium dips slightly (a few mmol/L) then normalises within hours in a healthy person.
Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus sense the dilution and suppress both thirst and ADH release — the body is actively telling you to stop.

timeline.headline: Sodium dips if salt intake is low; sleep fragmented by nocturia

effects.note: Continuous maximal dilution. Sodium, potassium and some water-soluble vitamins are lost in the large urine volume; the kidney compensates but the margin narrows on a low-salt diet.
Mild dilutional hyponatraemia causes low-grade headache, fogginess and nausea in susceptible people — brain cells take up water and swell slightly inside a rigid skull.
Nocturia 2–3 times a night; the bladder's functional capacity is unchanged but the filling rate overwhelms it.
No measurable 'glow' beyond what adequate hydration already gives; skin hydration is limited by the epidermal barrier, not by how much you drink past normal.

timeline.headline: Kidneys adapt; risk depends entirely on sweat and salt

effects.note: The renal medulla's concentration gradient washes out with chronic high water flow, so the kidney becomes slightly less able to concentrate urine on a day you drink less — this reverses in days.
Blood pressure is essentially unchanged in healthy people; the extra water is excreted rather than retained.
Aldosterone rises modestly to hold on to sodium as urinary losses continue — an adaptation, not harm.

timeline.headline: Steady state: harmless if active and salted, wasteful if sedentary

effects.note: No structural change. Kidney function tests (creatinine, eGFR) stay normal; there is no evidence that high water intake 'cleans' or improves healthy kidneys beyond preventing stones.
Frequent voiding persists. Some people train themselves to hold larger volumes, which can mildly increase bladder capacity but is not a health benefit.
In the low-salt, sedentary, or SSRI/thiazide-taking subgroup, chronic mild hyponatraemia subtly impairs attention and balance — often mistaken for tiredness.

timeline.headline: Stone risk lower; no other measurable benefit over 3 L

effects.note: High urine volume keeps calcium oxalate and uric acid below saturation, so the one clear benefit is fewer kidney stones — relevant in the hot, stone-prone 'stone belt' of north-west India. But ~2.5–3 L of urine a day is enough for this; 5 L adds little.
Urinary calcium loss rises slightly with large urine volumes; on an adequate calcium diet this has no bone effect, but it is another reason 5 L is not 'free'.
Stool softening plateaus; beyond adequate hydration, extra water is absorbed and excreted by the kidneys, not the gut.

timeline.headline: Same picture: excess excreted, hyponatraemia the only real risk

effects.note: One year of 5 L/day leaves healthy kidneys structurally unchanged. Slight enlargement of urine-handling capacity is functional, not anatomical.

Cumulative risk is a single bad day — a fever, vomiting, or a marathon of drinking at a wedding on top of 5 L habit — when sodium can fall below 125 mmol/L and cause seizures. The habit lowers the buffer.
Persistent high-frequency voiding; nocturia keeps fragmenting deep sleep for people who front-load water in the evening.

timeline.headline: No long-term organ damage; no long-term benefit beyond 3 L

effects.note: Long-term cohort data (e.g. large observational studies of high fluid intake) show neither faster decline nor extra protection of kidney function in healthy people once intake exceeds ~2.5–3 L. The extra 2 L is work with no return.

For outdoor labourers in Indian heat, 5 L with salt over five years is simply correct hydration and prevents heat illness. For the sedentary, it is a harmless-but-pointless ritual — unless one of the risk conditions in the caution appears.
With age, kidneys lose some ability to excrete free water and medication use (BP tablets, antidepressants) rises — so the same 5 L habit that was harmless at 30 carries more hyponatraemia risk at 60.
